significance.justification: Verified true, the claim would establish a form-(iii) law: "transfer ... is a monotone function of typological distance," with semantic and syntactic components governed by different measurable sub-distances; this would predict an ordering of retained causal effects for language pairs and explain why particular component classes transfer differently. This establishes both a cross-lingual transfer phenomenon and a mechanistic-level regularity, materially constraining observations beyond one component, unlike the task-level similarity correlations used in Pires et al. (2019) and Lauscher et al. (2020). Verified false would reject typological distance as a general predictive account of circuit and feature reuse, although failure of only one component-distance pairing would not cleanly distinguish a wholly false law from a narrower one; true and false are nevertheless distinguishable because monotonicity and the proposed dissociation are definite. The topic-substitution check lowers no score: multilingual representation alone would not imply this specific monotone, feature-type-dependent law, which is sharper than the topic-median hypothesis that some representations are shared while others are language-specific.

reach.justification: The named handles are the "per-component transfer score (target-language causal effect / source effect)" and the mapping from component type to typological sub-distance, which together could predict "which languages will fail to inherit which capabilities." This is potentially ex ante because known typological distances can flag risky source-target pairs before attempting transfer, leaving an action window for language selection or targeted multilingual improvement, rather than merely explaining an observed failure afterward. The monotone relation and dimension-specific ordering should survive per-model re-extraction better than a particular steering vector, but the hypothesis does not explicitly assert invariance across architectures, scales, or training regimes, so its stated uptake is strongest for multilingual-model researchers and practitioners choosing or auditing transfer paths rather than as a universal deployment rule. The topic-substitution check also supports an above-median score: deleting the distance law and its predictive score would leave only the broad multilingual-transfer topic and no comparable screening handle.
